entry.title: The stress test
entry.content:
The stress test

India's AI opportunity does not become serious by avoiding pressure. It becomes serious by turning pressure into a system that can deliver. Export access, currency, memory, packaging, power, fibre and the buyer's income all meet in the same workload. A campus can be impressive and still fail because one of those connections breaks.

In September 2025, I brought the buyer and the buildout together with the operating requirements to ask what happens when the conditions turn against them. Which part of the promise breaks first, and what would let useful work continue?

There are three external pressures: the strategic control of capability, the currency in which it is financed, and the geography of its supply chain. Inside India, they meet five practical constraints: power, storage, fibre routes, compliance and operating efficiency. The buyer's capacity to pay runs through the whole account.

Deterrence can make cooperation rational

A state will not treat frontier computing as an ordinary commodity if it believes the same capacity can change military or strategic power. My reading is that credible limits, verification and mutual dependence can make cooperation more rational than an unrestricted race. Cixin Liu's dark forest is a useful image of the fear: when another actor's intentions and future capabilities are uncertain, restraint becomes difficult to trust.

It remains an analogy, not a model that proves a particular export policy will produce peace. The practical question is whether access arrangements create a credible route for legitimate capability while constraining uses the parties regard as unacceptable. An indefinite, unpredictable queue can damage that bargain as surely as a completely unenforced promise.

The January 2025 US AI Diffusion Rule tried to structure access through country groupings and authorisations affecting advanced computing and certain model weights. It cannot be described as a settled rule operating unchanged in September. On 13 May 2025, BIS announced that the new compliance requirements would not be enforced and that rescission and replacement were planned.1 Its May 2026 guidance distinguished that non-enforcement policy from pre-existing controls that remain applicable to specified entities and transactions.2 On 19 November 2026 an interim final rule formally rescinded the Diffusion Rule. In its place, BIS requires licences for advanced chips bound for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, and controls exports to overseas data centres that supply significant compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. India is not among the named destinations.3

Access is conditional, and the condition can move. India's negotiating objective should be predictable access with credible safeguards and clear responsibilities. I called the desired middle ground “Tier 1.5”: a proposal for a practical relationship, not the name of a legal category or an entitlement that an Indian buyer can claim.

The effect of delay is larger than a chip's purchase price. It can idle a completed facility, consume a product window or force a different model and topology. Predictability is therefore part of productive capacity.

Currency moves through contracts and calendars

A domestic service earning rupees and purchasing equipment in dollars becomes more expensive to build when the rupee weakens, unless another arrangement offsets that exposure. A GCC earning dollars can receive more rupees for the same foreign receipt. Those consequences can coexist. There is no single sign attached to “India benefits from depreciation.”

In an illustrative example, a USD 100,000 equipment payment costs ₹83 lakh at ₹83 per dollar and ₹90 lakh at ₹90. The difference is ₹7 lakh. A USD 100,000 receipt due at the same time could offset that particular currency exposure before other costs. The same receipt due six months later leaves today's funding problem intact. Matching annual totals is not matching cash when it is needed. The rupee has since weakened past the example's ₹90 per dollar: FBIL's reference rate first fixed above it on 3 December 2025 and stood at ₹94.12 on 16 November 2026.4

The contract determines who feels the move first. A fixed-price supplier can lose margin while a supplier able to pass the cost through raises the customer's bill. The customer may then reduce demand. Financing costs, hedging, working capital and credit risk sit between the exchange-rate chart and the final outcome. The payment map makes those paths visible.

This reaches households too. A stronger export receipt does not automatically raise the wage of every worker, and more expensive imports can squeeze budgets elsewhere. Household financial saving is one useful aggregate, but gross assets, net saving and accumulated wealth answer different questions. None substitutes for the monthly cash flow that lets a family keep buying and investing through a transition.

A token does not remove the underlying claim

The growth of tokenised real-world assets extends the same question into financial infrastructure. A token representing a claim on cash, Treasury bills or a fund still depends on custody, redemption, the issuer, the assets and the applicable rules. Changing the record or settlement mechanism does not dissolve those dependencies.

The US executive order of 6 March 2025 established a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve initially capitalised with qualifying forfeited bitcoin and allowed the development of budget-neutral acquisition strategies. It did not order a sale of the country's gold reserves to buy bitcoin.5 Treating that more dramatic possibility as a scenario can test how reserve preferences might affect currencies and capital flows; presenting it as an enacted instruction would be false.

For India, the question is how a change in settlement, reserves or collateral would reach the cost and availability of capital. A plausible transmission path deserves analysis. A striking asset-price story does not supply the probability of the scenario, and no reserve narrative makes an individual holding an automatic hedge.

The chip is a chain, not a single object

A leading accelerator relies on memory, packaging, fabrication, substrates and equipment from a concentrated set of capabilities. Buying the processor does not create another source of high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which supplies data to the processor at the rate demanding AI workloads need. Nor does every assembly-and-test plant perform the advanced packaging required by the same system.

That distinction matters for India's semiconductor progress. Micron's Sanand project was an assembly-and-test investment for DRAM and NAND products. In February 2026 the company reported its opening and commercial production, converting wafers from its global manufacturing network into finished memory and storage products.6 That is real later progress, but it is not evidence that Sanand supplies every HBM or advanced-packaging requirement of an AI accelerator.

Micron separately announced a Singapore HBM packaging facility in January 2025, with operations scheduled to begin in 2026 and meaningful additional packaging capacity from 2027.7 In September 2026 Micron expected the plant's initial output in early 2027.8 TSMC's 2024 annual account described continued expansion of Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate (CoWoS), its advanced packaging technology for integrating chips, and other advanced capacity in Taiwan.9 Those are distinct stages and locations in a supply chain, not interchangeable instances of “a chip factory.”

Domestic assembly, testing and packaging can build valuable skills and relationships. The next step is to identify which dependence each project actually reduces. Counting facilities without their capabilities can make the country appear more independent than the workload is.

Minerals and mundane equipment have leverage too

Strategic concentration extends beyond semiconductors. China's July 2023 announcement introduced licensing for specified gallium and germanium items from August.10 That was not an unconditional ban on every export of either element. It nevertheless illustrated how access to a small material input can become a negotiating instrument. A later step singled out one destination: in December 2024 China said it would in principle refuse licences to export both elements to the United States, and in November 2025 suspended that rule until 27 November 2026, leaving the licensing in place.11 The treatment of any later shipment depends on the current item, destination and rules.

The response can also be contractual. In July 2025, MP Materials announced a US Department of Defense arrangement with a ten-year price floor for its neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) products, materials used in powerful permanent magnets, and commitments supporting magnet production.12 That is a specific effort to make alternative supply financeable, not proof that a price floor for every critical mineral has been enacted. Wider price-floor discussions should be read as proposals until their own rules exist.

Copper, aluminium, cables and transformers make the connection to a data centre less glamorous and more direct. A forecast of a future material shortage is conditional on demand, substitution and new supply. The procurement queue is already an operating constraint: the IEA's February 2025 survey reported two-to-three-year cable procurement and up to four years for large power transformers.13 These were survey findings, not the promised lead time for every Indian order.

An order book can therefore precede usable capacity by years. A subsidy that ignores the enabling equipment may fund machines that wait for the thing that lets them turn on.

Two routes must fail differently

Subsea cables and their landing infrastructure connect India's services to distant customers. A new route can add capacity and resilience without removing exposure to shared seas, landing stations or terrestrial corridors. Two carrier names can still pass through the same vulnerable geography.

The useful test is physical: trace the routes, identify the shared points, rehearse failover and measure the result. A longer alternate path may restore connectivity while missing the application's latency target. For a training job, moving data or rebuilding a checkpoint on the alternate service can dominate recovery. For an interactive service, requests keep arriving while the infrastructure is being repaired.

Resilience belongs to the customer's completed work. It is not established by the existence of a second supplier or a green dashboard.

Power has both a near horizon and a long one

The immediate problem is firm electricity, a connection, storage and an operating design that survives the conditions actually expected at the site. National storage projections need their components intact: CEA's 411.4 GWh requirement for 2031–32 combined 175.18 GWh of pumped storage with 236.22 GWh of batteries. The power calculation also distinguishes delivered energy from nameplate storage.

Thorium belongs to a longer horizon. India's three-stage nuclear programme gives it a strategic place through the production and use of fissile material; the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE)'s account of the fast-breeder programme makes that sequence explicit.14 Its Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) research explores a thorium-based reactor design.15 The Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam reached first criticality on 6 April 2026, a second-stage milestone that comes before it supplies power to the grid.16 A research design, fuel-cycle programme and commissioned supply are different stages.

That long-run possibility deserves investment without being used as today's electricity contract. An AI workload due in FY27 cannot draw from a reactor that has not been commissioned for it. Conversely, today's grid constraint does not prove long-horizon research is pointless. The clocks must remain distinct.

Compliance and efficiency are capabilities

Predictable access to customers depends on knowing what data can be used, who is accountable and what happens when something goes wrong. In September 2025 the rules under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act were still discussed through the draft process. That description is now historical: final rules and a staged commencement framework were notified in November 2025. Some provisions began immediately, others after one year and a substantial group after eighteen months.17 The consent-manager provisions began on 13 November 2026, and the eighteen-month group begins on 13 May 2027. It would be equally misleading to call the whole framework a draft or to say every obligation was already in force by November 2026.

The practical aim is readiness: data handling, contracts, incident response and an accountable operating team. A compliance document cannot substitute for those behaviours, but uncertain obligations and last-minute redesign can become a real cost of delivery.

Efficiency is another way to turn pressure into capacity. Model FLOPs utilisation (MFU) compares useful model arithmetic per second with the hardware’s relevant theoretical peak. My proposed training-service gate remains median MFU of at least 0.50 on a declared reference workload, paired with visible allocation windows and queue reporting. A proposed queue target below twenty-four hours needs a specified request class and observation period. Neither number is an empirical claim about the whole Indian market. The procurement proposal explains what each measurement would have to establish.

Recovery is more than the outage

Consider a training run interrupted for four hours. The last usable checkpoint is two hours old. After power returns, replacement capacity takes three more hours to become ready, and restart validation takes one hour. If those stages happen sequentially and useful training then resumes at the same rate, completion slips by:

ΔT=4+3+1+2=10 hours. \Delta T=4+3+1+2=10\,\mathrm{hours}.

The final two hours are repeated computation, not additional outage. Parallel recovery could shorten the total. An incompatible replacement could make the run impossible. The example is stipulated; it shows why an availability percentage does not determine whether a deadline survives.

For an inference service, the equivalent question includes the backlog that accumulated during failure. A recovered machine can still serve users too slowly. The acceptance test must follow the service back to its useful state.

Keep the buyer in the picture

The infrastructure can recover technically while its business does not. A delayed customer can abandon an experiment, use a substitute or find that the expected gain no longer justifies the bill. GCC demand can support employment and local services, but its absorption of displaced workers depends on skills, location and timing.

There is a larger limit too. If automation narrows some income streams, cheaper output does not guarantee that all households can buy more. Exports, public expenditure and ownership income can support different buyers. Purchasing power is part of the production system's durability.

My policy preference is therefore concrete: negotiate predictable access; commission firm power and genuinely diverse routes; publish comparable queue and MFU evidence; prepare institutions for their obligations; and build applications that strengthen useful work and household capability. Storage guarantees or viability-gap support should be judged by delivered service, not only by announced support. The private investment question then follows the actual contracts and exposures rather than assigning every adjacent business the same future. Own the bridge, not the trophy develops that discipline.

The question of what an architecture can ultimately understand belongs alongside this operating inquiry, not inside a GPU count. Beyond the Mirage makes that separate argument. One Yardstick, One Clock asks when measured capability becomes an economic substitute and what room remains to adapt.

Pressure is useful when it tells us where the bridge needs reinforcement. An export constraint should lead to a clearer access arrangement; a supply bottleneck to an honest delivery sequence; a household warning to a better account of demand. India's opportunity is to make those responses repeatable enough that useful work continues when the easy assumptions stop holding.

entry.title: Tracing the infrastructure story
entry.content:
Tracing the infrastructure story

My interest in India's AI infrastructure began with a question about markets: if this transformation requires so much capital, where would its economic value appear?

At first, the answer seems to be a map of obvious dependencies. AI needs chips, electricity, buildings, networks and cooling. Each dependency suggests a business. But a list of necessary inputs is not yet an account of who benefits, how much they retain or whether the price already assumes that benefit. That distinction gradually became more interesting to me than the portfolio itself. It connects infrastructure to ownership, contracts and the distribution of a productive gain.

Necessity and return travel along different paths

Suppose a campus cannot operate without a grid connection. The connection is necessary, but its necessity alone says little about the return to any particular electricity business. A regulated network, a competitive generator, an equipment supplier and the campus operator can all participate in supplying power while facing different pricing rules, costs and risks. Demand for their function does not translate into the same economic claim for each of them.

The same is true of the building. Owning nearby office space does not make a property owner a claimant on the campus's computing revenue. Even owning a suitable facility produces a particular rental or service relationship, not a share of every profit its tenant earns.

The chain has at least two maps. The operating map shows what the workload depends on. The economic map shows what each participant is entitled to receive and what they must supply in return. A convincing thesis needs both.

Contracts determine who bears interruption, replacement and maintenance obligations, and how long a claim lasts. Equipment depreciation also affects what the participant retains from a payment. The customer relationship has its own acceptance conditions, payment terms and remedies, and depends on continuing demand.

A necessary input is not a share of the profit. Costs, risks and timing change each contractual claim; “this is needed” does not establish “this participant captures the value.”

The contract changes the exposure

Two apparently similar suppliers can have opposite exposures to the same event. Imagine two illustrative capacity contracts. One supplier promises a fixed price for a year while buying a significant input at a variable price. Another passes that input cost through to its customer. A rise in the input price squeezes the first supplier's margin directly; the second may preserve its unit margin but lose demand as the customer's bill rises. Neither is simply “an AI beneficiary.” Their consequences depend on the contract.

Timing also matters. An equipment order can create revenue for a supplier before the campus produces a useful result. A recurring service provider earns only while the relationship continues. A financier may be paid a contractual return while still bearing credit risk if the project fails. These positions meet at one campus but do not share one payoff.

This is the weakness in treating a sector label as a causal explanation. The label groups firms by a story. It does not reveal their claims on the story's outcome.

The horizon changes what the same asset means

An input that is scarce during a construction rush can become abundant after supply expands. The company selling it may benefit from the bottleneck without retaining the same advantage once the bottleneck eases. Conversely, an expensive early investment can be commercially disappointing while creating a capability that proves valuable later. The original investor and the later user need not be the same beneficiary. These possibilities make a boom difficult to summarise with one valuation. Financing, construction, operation and later reuse happen at different times. Their gains and losses can be distributed among different people.

The IEA's April 2026 analysis describes constraints in chips, grid connections and energy equipment within its discussion of AI's energy demand.1 Those are specific supply constraints, not a promise that every business adjacent to them earns an exceptional return.

The distinction follows the story into an investment product too. A company can supply an essential component while earning most of its revenue elsewhere; two funds can carry the same supplier under different labels. Following the holdings back to the business makes that another question, rather than treating a convincing campus as a convincing security.

A thesis needs a way to change

The map can also make revision less arbitrary. In the fixed-price supplier example, suppose the thesis depends on demand filling the contracted capacity and input costs remaining within a stated range. Before the next observation, specify what would count against each link: repeated empty bookings would challenge demand, while an input-price rise with no contractual pass-through would challenge the retained margin. A rise in the security's price would establish neither condition.

Those observations can lead to different revisions. Evidence of durable demand might preserve the workload thesis while weaker margin retention changes which participant is a convincing proxy for it. A new contract could alter that conclusion again. An unknown business mix should widen the uncertainty rather than be filled with a favourable estimate. This is a research discipline for the argument, not an automatic instruction to trade.

The loop is therefore thesis, observable condition, comparison and revision. Deciding in advance which condition would change which conclusion makes it harder to explain every later event as confirmation. It also preserves the useful part of a thesis when one link fails: the computing service can be real while the proposed claim on its value was wrong.

Foreign revenue can arrive without broad domestic benefit

An export-oriented computing service introduces another split. Its customers may pay from abroad while much of its equipment is imported. Some value stays in wages, local services, taxes and domestic ownership returns; some pays for the imported inputs and foreign claims. The balance is not captured by pointing at the export receipt alone. Nor does a company earning foreign currency establish that all the households around it have acquired greater purchasing power.

This is why the national infrastructure story eventually led me to the questions in Post-AGI Economics. Productive capacity, the claims on that capacity and the demand for its output belong in the same account. Otherwise a gain in one place can be mistaken for a gain everywhere.

From an asset map to a transmission map

The useful object is not a shopping list of companies. It is a transmission map: this workload requires this input; this participant supplies it; this relationship determines the payment; this cost or risk remains with that participant; and this group eventually receives the gain.

Such a map also makes disagreement productive. One person can accept the growth of a workload while doubting a supplier's ability to retain its margin. Another can believe that a campus will operate successfully while questioning how widely its benefits will spread. They are disagreeing about different links, not necessarily about the existence of AI.

The claim on value sits on an operating chain, and its durability depends on what happens when that chain is disrupted. A component can be physically necessary while another participant holds the contract, currency exposure or residual income. Mapping those relationships connects the infrastructure story to the economic claim someone actually owns. That is the change in my own inquiry: from finding assets near a compelling story to understanding what actually carries the story's value.

  1. IEA's energy and AI analysis. ↩

entry.title: What the IndiaAI compute numbers count
entry.content:
What the IndiaAI compute numbers count

In two official August 2026 accounts, the same 237 projects and 93.18 lakh GPU-hours occupied different positions in the story. One described approved projects and sanctioned hours. The other described projects that had accessed subsidised computing. A change in the verb can sound like a change in delivery, even when the number stays the same.

This investigation follows programme reports and allocation-register observations through 24 September 2026. It asks a narrow question: what can those public records establish about the conversion of promised compute into useful work? The observation period matters because a later consumption report could answer a question these records leave open.

The verb changes the event

The 6 August parliamentary answer reports 237 projects approved for subsidised support and 93.18 lakh GPU-hours sanctioned. The 13 August factsheet calls the same figures accessed compute. It separately reports 62 prototypes and 20 deployed solutions. Neither supplies a project-level reconciliation connecting those hours to those outputs.

Approval can establish eligibility for support. Sanction can establish an allocation. Access can mean that an applicant has a usable route into the service. Consumption would record actual use. An output would identify what that use produced. These events can occur close together, but no arithmetic lets one count substitute for the others without knowing the reporting definition.

The question is consequential for a buyer or programme operator. If an allocation expires before a workload starts, the approved hours did not become consumed hours. If a run starts and repeatedly fails, consumption can increase without a usable model or completed experiment. Conversely, a small efficient run can produce valuable output with fewer hours. A favourable count at one stage can accompany very different outcomes at the next.

A start-by date is an obligation

The compute portal's allocation register, observed on 3 and 24 September, provided columns for applicants, providers, allocated equipment, project duration, allocation dates and start-by dates. With project rows, those fields would identify who received an award and when use was expected to begin. The observed columns did not report consumed hours, expiry, queueing, service reliability, completion or attributable output for the same projects.

The seven user-category counters summed to 301 on 3 September and 304 on 24 September: two more Startups & MSMEs and one more Early-stage startup. Those are changes in the portal’s user counters, not a consumption series or a reconciliation of the 237 projects. The saved calculation below compares the counters, the allocation fields and the two August reports. Both captured tables retain their headings but no project rows; those were requested separately by the page. The dated responses needed to match individual projects are missing.

The client script used a startusedate field to populate the start-by column. A field name alone cannot establish that a workload actually started. The public presentation has to tell us which event is being recorded.

An allocation service-level commitment also answers a narrower question than a workload guarantee. Promising to allocate a request within a stated window does not establish uninterrupted execution or completion by a customer's deadline. The capacity promise needs its own clock: when the job can start, what happens after an interruption and which remedy applies if the window is missed.

One provider's trace from allocated compute to released models

The evidence is not all unresolved allocation. In its 6 March model release, Sarvam says it trained its 30B and 105B models in India on IndiaAI compute, released their weights and put them into production services. Its earlier Indus launch described limited-beta access and a waitlist under constrained compute capacity.

That account connects supplied compute to identifiable model artifacts and services, while also showing that service access can remain constrained after the model exists. It is a provider's account of particular outputs, not an independently reconciled conversion rate for all programme-supported projects. It nevertheless prevents the national argument from collapsing into “nothing was delivered.” Some useful work can be visible while the portfolio-wide denominator remains unresolved.

The strongest alternative is reporting lag

Perhaps the sanctioned hours had already become real use, and “accessed” was a reasonable shorthand for that transition. Perhaps the prototypes and deployments were early results that simply had not been joined to the compute register publicly. That would be a reporting gap rather than a delivery failure. The absence of the join cannot decide which explanation is right.

A useful next table would follow the same supported project cohort from approved or sanctioned hours into started and consumed hours, expired or cancelled allocations, service performance, completed work and output identifiers. It would state the observation interval and define the stages. Projects whose completion takes longer should remain visible as continuing work rather than disappear from the denominator.

That table could change the conclusion in either direction. Reliable conversion within the promised windows would show that the administrative counts are a useful leading account of delivery. Large non-starts or repeated interruption would reveal where the bridge is failing. Without it, the figures establish support and access more clearly than the rate at which that support becomes completed work.

The physical chain explains what makes usable compute possible. The reporting chain has to connect that possibility to an actual workload. Neither a national GPU count nor a suspicious reading of a headline can finish the investigation on its own.

entry.title: The relationship inside the account
entry.content:
The relationship inside the account

A customer has two opportunities in progress: one team is exploring a new service while another renews an existing engagement. Someone maintains continuity across the account, someone handles each opportunity, and someone else can promise delivery. Which of them is "the owner"?

An organisation chart cannot answer that question alone. The useful unit is the particular relationship: what somebody may promise, why the customer is interested, who carries the next responsibility and who can accept its result. A commercial system becomes more intelligible when those relationships have room to be recorded in their own right, instead of competing for one field. Weave is designed to carry that commercial world together with the work it creates, for people and agents alike.

Continuity and mandate answer different questions

The account manager can preserve the relationship's history: who matters, which concerns recur and what has previously been agreed. An account executive can handle a defined commercial mandate. The two live opportunities still need their own responsibilities and permissions.

Relationship in the example Responsibility Interval or boundary
Account continuity Maintain history and coordinate the customer's recurring concerns Across both opportunities and later handovers
New-service opportunity Qualify the proposed work and carry its agreed next step This opportunity, under its mandate
Renewal opportunity Resolve the existing service's renewal question This renewal, not every future sale
Delivery authority Accept a commitment the team can fulfil The particular scope and terms approved

One person may hold several of these roles. The record still needs to say which relationship they are acting on. A change in the renewal contact should not rewrite who qualified the new service, and an account-wide conversation should not quietly commit the delivery team. Weave's intended commercial model gives accounts, people, opportunities, mandates and dated relationships separate objects so those changes remain intelligible.

Finding a fit that can become work

Consider the same account over three reviews. During discovery, the new-service sponsor describes recurring delays and the operating owner offers access to the relevant records. The opportunity has a plausible problem and a way to investigate it. At the next review, the proposed access is unavailable, so the assessment becomes blocked even though the sponsor remains interested. Later, a narrower dataset becomes available and a revised scope can be assessed. The original interest did not disappear; the means of delivering the proposed work changed.

Weave's commercial design keeps those assessments with the evidence, reviewer and policy version that produced each one. The current queue shows the narrower next step and who is pursuing it, while the earlier assessments explain why the team did not proceed sooner. Renewal work at that account continues throughout. Its mandate, sponsor and evidence are different, even if the account manager is the same person.

That history is useful commercially. It distinguishes a lost opportunity from an access problem, a delayed response from a rejected proposal, and a changed scope from an unexplained drop in score. Buyer, sponsor, technical owner and operating owner become relationships to investigate and maintain, not four extra contact fields whose names imply responsibility.

A promising opportunity is not necessarily an eligible one. Suppose a customer wants a service that the team could technically deliver, but the requested use violates an established boundary. A high opportunity score cannot cancel that disqualifier.

Even for eligible work, a reviewer needs the evidence for and against the fit, including what has gone stale and what is still unknown. Without it, a score can make an unsettled judgment look like measured truth. Weave keeps the policy and evidence behind each assessment as they stood at the time. If a later conversation changes the judgment, the new conclusion supersedes the old one without deleting it. The team can then distinguish a poor original decision from a reasonable decision made before the situation changed.

From a suggested step to an accepted obligation

An analysis might recommend scheduling a workshop. Before that becomes a commitment, the team and customer need to agree its terms, with someone authorised to commit the team. Until then, it remains a proposed next action with reasons. Moving a card across a board cannot make that agreement for them.

A small team with clear standing authority may need only a concise record of the agreement. The authority is already there, so the process can be light. Silence alone cannot establish it.

Returning to the account

The next account review can now begin somewhere definite. The renewal is proceeding under its existing mandate. The new service has a narrower dataset and a proposed workshop, with a named person still needed to accept that work. The account manager can carry that history into the conversation without promising delivery on either opportunity's behalf.

The two teams also need different parts of the history. The renewal team may need the customer's recurring concern but not the new-service team's restricted technical records. A useful shared picture connects those references while showing where a team has to ask for access. Weave's intended model would make that position available to people and to Pale: what changed, which commitment remains and who can take the next step. One account can then have continuity without forcing every opportunity, promise and private conversation into one owner field.

entry.title: Turning a conversation into work
entry.content:
Turning a conversation into work

Work often starts before anyone calls it work. A customer mentions a problem, a colleague offers to investigate and a manager says it sounds useful. Three weeks later, everyone remembers a different commitment. What, exactly, did we agree to do?

Somewhere in that conversation, a suggestion needed to become a responsibility somebody accepted. Finding that moment is one of the questions behind Weave. People and agents should be able to continue the work without rereading an entire conversation to decide which remark became a promise.

The responsibility inside the exchange

Imagine a team discussing an unreliable export. One person says, “I can look at the timeout.” Another says, “We also need a better error message.” Both would improve the export. But the investigation can finish while the error message stays exactly as it was. A different person might accept the interface change. These are two responsibilities we can assign and accept separately.

For each, keep a short account of the work, who is taking it and what would let someone accept the result. Link the conversation that explains why it matters. The person who turns the suggestion into work is its creator; the original speaker remains the source of the suggestion. An agent reading the transcript needs the same distinction. Spotting an action is useful. Assigning it to somebody requires permission to do so.

Ordinary discussion and accountable change

Now somebody writes “done”. Is the investigation done? Is the patch ready? Has the customer accepted the result? Before changing the record, the system needs to know which responsibility the person means and whether they can make that decision. They should be able to decide in the conversation where they are already working.

Small teams can make these distinctions verbally. A formal system becomes useful when work crosses time, organisational boundaries or several independently acting participants. The point is to preserve the agreed meaning, not to impose ceremony on every helpful exchange.

In the export example, “I can look at the timeout” could become an agreed investigation: reproduce the timeout on the stated export, report its cause or the missing evidence, and return that result to the person accepting the investigation. “We need a better error message” remains a separate proposed change until someone takes it. When the investigator says “done” and supplies a trace, the investigation is ready for its agreed acceptance; the interface change has not magically finished alongside it.

The reviewer could reply to that investigation, “Accepted: this trace answers the timeout investigation.” In Weave's design, that message carries the decision. The reviewer's identity must be bound to someone entitled to accept this exact work, and the supplied result must meet the agreed conditions. The same checks apply whether the decision arrives through chat or another interface. Once they pass, acceptance is recorded and the work's card updates; the reviewer is not asked to confirm again. A repeated delivery of the message must not produce a second acceptance. If the message leaves the item unclear, the system asks which one is meant. If the reviewer lacks authority or a condition is unmet, it explains the refusal where the decision was made and leaves the work unchanged.

If an attempted closure lacks that acceptance, Weave's intended response is to keep the item open and identify the missing condition. The refusal is useful because it preserves the team's agreement. The investigator can supply the absent result or ask for the agreement to change, rather than losing the distinction under a successful status update.

The resulting history is small but consequential:

In the illustrative export investigation What the work record retains
A colleague suggests looking at the timeout The source exchange, still a proposal
An authorised participant creates the investigation That participant as creator, with the original speaker and message kept as the source
An investigator takes the work The assignment, current attempt and agreed result
The investigator posts a trace and writes “done” The comment and supplied result, without silently closing the item
The entitled reviewer accepts the stated investigation in an unambiguous reply One recorded acceptance and an updated card, without another confirmation

The suggested interface fix remains beside the completed investigation. We have an answer about the timeout; somebody still needs to take on the proposed error-message change. The two records let the team see both.

Handover changes the future, not the past

Suppose the investigator leaves the role. Work nobody has started can move to the verified successor. Work already in progress stops accepting new effort until the handover is agreed: establish what has happened, what permission still applies and what the successor is taking on. The completed timeout investigation keeps the person who did it. Replacing their name everywhere would tidy the task list by making its history false. The handover needs its own record, whether work passes between two people, a person and an agent, or two agents.

Recurring work has a related boundary. “Review this every month” is a schedule; this month's review is an occurrence. One successful occurrence cannot stand for the next, and a missed occurrence needs an explicit policy rather than disappearing behind the schedule's active status.

What closes the responsibility

The task should close against its agreed result, not because the conversation went quiet. A provider can supply a result while the consumer still disputes its adequacy. Delivery and acceptance need to remain visible separately. At the next month's review, this month's result should have its own acceptance, the next occurrence its own responsibility, and a handover its account of what the earlier participant actually did. Conversation can remain informal because the record carries the commitments that need to survive it. The team can then return to discussing the problem, rather than arguing over which remark became a promise.

entry.title: Two meanings of done
entry.content:
Two meanings of done

The comparison arrives on time. The file opens, the tables are readable, and the analyst has handed over what they promised. The recipient opens it to make a decision and finds that it compares the wrong population.

Suppose this was the comparison you commissioned. You have the file, but you still cannot make the decision. The analyst needs to know what arrived and what needs correcting. Calling the whole thing "done" or "not done" gives neither of you enough to continue.

The file arrived. Did it answer the need?

Delivery concerns the promised artifact; acceptance concerns the agreed question and criteria. The recipient may accept the comparison, reject it with reasons or identify a specific piece of work still missing. Those possibilities give the handoff a future: the delivered file remains available, and the particular failure can become a defined revision rather than another ambiguous request to "fix it".

Suppose the decision concerns renewal among existing customers, but the table combines them with people trying the product for the first time. The recipient can say: “The file arrived. I need the existing-customer cohort separated before this can support the renewal decision.” That response recognises the delivery and gives the analyst a specific correction. “This is useless” would discard the useful part; “done” would carry the wrong population into the next decision.

A child task does not close its parent's goal

An application can report that it wrote a file. A deployment system can report that it uploaded a build. Neither alone proves that the intended reader can use the document or that the approved website is being served correctly. The parent goal has its own completion conditions. It can use the child's evidence without replacing those conditions with the easiest observable success signal. Otherwise a green step conceals unfinished work at the next boundary.

Acceptance must belong to someone

In the renewal example, the operating owner responsible for the decision applies the agreed criterion: existing customers, the relevant renewal period and an explanation of who was excluded. The analyst revises the cohort, preserves the original delivered comparison and sends the corrected version with its changed denominator. If the criterion is met, the owner can accept that comparison as sufficient for the renewal analysis. The subsequent decision about what to offer those customers is still another act.

This also limits a disagreement. If the recipient now wants a different period or a trial-customer analysis, that can become new work rather than an endlessly moving acceptance test. A partial acceptance can close the correct cohort table while leaving one disputed interpretation open. Naming the version, criterion and remaining question lets both people act without pretending that the entire business decision fitted inside a file-delivery event.

The supplier has a decision too

The analyst's team may review its own work before delivery. It can confirm that the calculation follows the chosen method, the file contains the requested tables and the stated exclusions are visible. That is a useful acceptance on the supplier's side. It does not give the team the customer's decision about whether the comparison is enough for the renewal analysis.

A publication makes the distinction particularly clear. Gazette can compose an article from its source, resolve its links and produce the pages. The person preparing the site can inspect those pages and establish that the requested build was delivered correctly. The publisher still has to accept the finished words, images and claims for release. After release, checking what readers actually receive answers another question again. A successful build is evidence for that sequence, not a substitute for the publisher's judgement.

In Pale's design, coordination keeps those results with the work they establish and leaves each acceptance with its owner. The same distinction matters when people use Gazette directly: a draft can be ready for review while publication remains undecided.

Closing the handoff

Making both events explicit gives each party something practical. The analyst can see that the handoff landed without waiting for it to stand for the entire decision. The recipient can see the outcome still needing judgement without erasing the work already delivered. If more work is needed, its reason can be stated precisely. A workflow closes through that agreement, rather than through whichever party first writes "done".

Unknown effects and interrupted work

A request to create a ticket leaves the caller, and the connection fails before the reply arrives. Somewhere on the other side, the ticket may already exist. The caller sees an error; the provider may have completed the work. What should happen next?

A retry feels like the natural repair because it makes the interface move again. But a new request can create a second ticket while leaving the first unexplained. Before trying again, the caller needs to find out whether the provider created the first ticket, or keep that question open if it cannot find out.

A log saying "timeout" tells us what happened to the connection, not what happened to the ticket. The same uncertainty appears in a payment, a deployment or a booking, though duplication has different consequences in each. Recovery therefore begins with the original request and the provider's state, rather than a fresh attempt whose apparent success could hide both effects.

An identity helps only if the provider honours it

A stable request identity can let a provider recognise repeated delivery of the same request, under a contract stating what is deduplicated, for how long and in which scope. Where the outcome remains ambiguous, a read-only lookup of that original request can turn the caller's uncertainty into a useful observation. It may confirm the effect, establish that it was not applied or leave the case open for another form of reconciliation.

Suppose the caller records request create-42 before sending it. The provider creates ticket T-19, but the reply is lost. Reading back create-42 can reveal T-19 if the provider supports that lookup. The useful next step is now to inspect that ticket, not to create T-20. If lookup is unavailable or inconclusive, the caller still has an unresolved request; a fresh identifier would conceal rather than settle it.

Give this fictional provider a more precise contract: it retains a create request's deduplication record for twenty-four hours, within the same account, and requires the same semantic body for a repeated key. Its ticket index is eventually updated. Those stipulations produce three different recovery observations:

Observation about create-42 What it establishes Where that leaves the work
Authoritative request lookup returns T-19 with the matching account and body The original creation occurred Inspect that ticket and continue from the observed result
An early search returns no ticket while the index may still be behind The search found nothing yet Creation remains unknown; preserve the original request and seek a stronger observation
The deduplication window expires before the result is resolved The provider no longer promises to recognise the key Creation remains unknown; a resubmission could now create another ticket

Caution

An expired key can allow a duplicate. The third row is particularly easy to misread. Expiry removes a recovery guarantee; it does not undo T-19 or prove it never existed. A retry with the same key can create a second ticket after the provider forgets the first request. Changing accounts can lose the guarantee even earlier. The recovery record therefore needs the account, original request and body, the provider's promised horizon and the observation that was actually obtained.

Pale’s effect path records the intention to dispatch before calling the provider. If the reply is lost, it keeps the outcome unresolved while the owner’s read-only check investigates what happened within its allowed scope and deadline. An inconclusive lookup leaves the case open. Evidence that the effect was not applied can support another course. A further change must stay within the owner’s existing permission or receive a new decision; changing the target or business action is not merely repairing the connection. Pale’s records for effects and reconciliation exist, but this complete path has not yet been proved against a real provider.

Recovery is still work

An unresolved effect needs an accountable place to remain open. Ending a session, cancelling a task or expiring a timeout does not make the external consequence disappear. Someone must own the next observation and any decision to accept, compensate or restore the provider's state. Compensation is itself another consequential action. It can require new authority, introduce a new failure and fail to restore every consequence of the first action. Calling it rollback does not make it harmless.

A recovery record is not accepted completion

Confirming that the ticket exists resolves the question of whether the create effect happened. It does not establish that the ticket is correct or that the broader workflow has achieved its purpose. Delivery and acceptance remain separate after reconciliation.

Pale's design gives an unknown effect a durable place in the work still owed. The same obligation exists in a manual process. A person following up an uncertain ticket needs to know which request to investigate and what observation would settle it. Reliable recovery preserves that unfinished question across the interruption.

entry.title: Finding the right context for the work
entry.content:
Finding the right context for the work

An agent returns to a task about a project and finds a compelling passage. It is the right subject, uses the right words and answers the question neatly. It is also from last year's arrangement, or from another organisation with a similar problem.

The puzzle is finding context that belongs to this work, not merely text that resembles it. A historical account and a current action can need different records about the same project. Scope is the ecosystem's cache for that task-specific account, sitting on Pale, Weave or both and, like any cache, optional and never the source of truth. It checks which records the task may use, keeps the facts needed to interpret them, and then ranks the useful detail. The result can be smaller than a broad search while carrying more of what matters. That includes the context around the people doing the work: which relationship a person is acting within, how a decision is made and which communication style fits the recipient. Finding a source and understanding its setting are complementary parts of useful memory.

What an agent needs to resume an essay

Scope’s first intended use is publication work: helping an agent resume an essay after a new session starts. The original writing establishes the argument; the current draft shows what has been developed; the publication's purpose explains why the piece belongs there; the current decisions identify what may change. A compressed account that remembers the title but loses the reason for the essay has preserved the wrong thing.

For a revision of Breath of Cosmos, the proposed slice could look like this:

Context Why this task needs it
The original breath-and-cosmos argument Preserve its passage from a breathing interval to an unbounded frame, including the textual image behind it
The current getHarsh edition See the developed argument and the qualifications beside its model of breath and consciousness
The distinct Sleepwalker reflection Keep the question about the observer and the world it can contain connected without making both essays the same piece
Current editorial decisions and the reuse terms of each image Distinguish a drafted revision from accepted publication, and an available image from one cleared for reuse

Note

Keep the originals within reach. Owner-supplied snapshots would help Scope assemble this context without replacing the full arguments an editor needs to read. Gazette has the separate job of presenting the resulting articles and their links; receiving this context would grant no permission to publish them.

Someone helping two organisations does not merge their records

Imagine someone helping two organisations with similar problems. The same operator and similar vocabulary can make their records look close in a semantic search. That does not make one organisation's private account an available example for the other. The request needs the relationship and purpose under which it is made, not just a query string. The source needs its own permitted uses. A system should not infer either from a familiar project name or the fact that the operator can technically open both files. The distinction also applies within one context. Information available for internal diagnosis may still be forbidden in a public explanation. A summary can carry the same restricted meaning in fewer words; compression does not clear the boundary.

Keep what the task needs before ranking the rest

Scope would first check which records the task may use and whether they are still valid and current enough. It would keep the required context, then rank optional material from the remaining records. A relevance score cannot bring an excluded source back. A small token budget cannot silently remove an authority page that changes the meaning of an otherwise attractive passage. The result may be a concise bundle with an authority page and two supporting passages rather than the ten closest excerpts. It may also be an explicitly limited answer because a necessary source is missing. Both are useful: the first carries enough context to interpret the evidence, while the second exposes the gap the task needs resolved.

For an imagined question about whether a service may be offered today, three passages could look equally relevant:

Candidate source Relation to this request Place in the bundle
Current offering decision Governs present availability Required, including its revision
Last year's promotional description Explains the historical proposition Optional history, labelled as such
Another organisation's private deployment Similar language, outside this request's source population Excluded before relevance ranking

A current decision saying the service is unavailable changes the reading of the historical description. Returning only the more fluent old passage would be a smaller answer, but a worse account of the task. The indispensable context is not always the nearest semantic match.

An exact reference could locate the current decision, while keyword search could find its terminology. Following links between permitted records, with a limit on how far the search goes, could reveal a relevant dependency. Model-assisted search could find a supporting passage that uses different words. Each method proposes material from what the caller is allowed to use; none changes that permission. Fixed rules could combine their rankings while keeping owner-pinned items and required context ahead of optional detail. Exact references, keyword search and links between records need no model.

Suppose a toy bundle has a 500-token budget. The required decision and its qualifying context cost 300 tokens, a supporting note costs 120, and a historical example costs 180. The decision plus the note fits at 420; adding the example reaches 600. The example can be omitted with its reason visible. If the indispensable context alone costs 600, ranking cannot solve the problem by discarding the qualification. The system needs a permitted larger budget or an answer that makes the unmet requirement explicit.

What reaches the answer besides the text

A system can omit restricted passages from the response while still using them to shape candidates or ranking. The existence of a result, a changed score or an observable count may then carry information that the caller was not meant to receive. The design must name the isolation it promises. Keeping restricted text out of the answer is one condition. Preventing restricted populations from changing the search result is stronger. Controlling information exposed through timing, caches, counts and errors is stronger again. Claiming the strongest condition because the weakest one passed would make the boundary fictional.

A filter applied after ranking can conceal restricted text while leaving its influence intact. Searching only a genuinely permitted population answers a different isolation question. The comparison between designs has to follow those information paths, rather than treating the label “filtered index” as a description of everything a caller can learn.

A relevant old statement can still be wrong for the task

Freshness is a relationship between a source, a request and a use. An old historical record can be exactly the right source for a historical question. The same record can be inadequate for a current action. A recent edit date does not verify every fact in a document. The response therefore needs to carry the revision and the limitation that matter. If a source has been revoked or a required authority has changed, an immutable cached answer does not become safe simply because its bytes are unchanged. The dependency has moved.

The context bundle should show what it leaves out

The aim is not to give every agent everything it might conceivably need. It is to give enough context for the particular task, with the sources, omissions and unresolved contradictions that change interpretation. A link to an original is valuable because it lets the reader inspect the reasoning, not because the link makes the summary authoritative. For the agent, the benefit is a shorter route to the right interpretation. It can inspect the source, see which revision supports the answer and notice a missing premise before acting on a fluent summary. Permission to make the eventual change remains with whoever owns the system where it is made; the bundle supplies the context needed to ask and reason well. Whether that bundle actually helped is a question about the work and its outcome, beyond the relevance score that selected it.

entry.title: When an agent's context changes underneath it
entry.content:
When an agent's context changes underneath it

An agent is drafting a product page from a decision to offer a service. Another agent records a new decision: the service is no longer being offered. The draft still reads well. Nobody has edited the same file, so there is no file conflict to catch. Yet publishing it would offer something that is no longer available.

Agents decide far more often than people, so by the time one writes, what it read has usually changed: the gap between the time of a read and the time of the action taken on it, which distributed systems have long handled as an occasional fault, becomes the ordinary case. Scope’s semantic-transaction research asks whether recording what the draft depends on would catch this kind of change better than a simpler system that checks source versions. The task is to notice the changed service decision while letting unrelated work continue.

The text being edited may be untouched

Call the drafting agent A and the agent recording the new decision B. To catch the problem, A's record of what it read must include the service decision and its revision. Recording only the draft file would miss the change. Recording merely the project name would not tell us which claim needs another look.

The same problem arises when an owner changes, a permission is revoked or a required contract is revised. Each can change what the draft may say or what someone may do with it. Keeping the particular dependency gives the check something to inspect; locking the whole project would also stop work that never relied on that decision.

Stale reasoning can continue as speculation

A may have written a useful explanation of how the service works. Pausing the offer does not necessarily make that explanation wrong. It does make the invitation to buy wrong. A can keep developing the draft as speculative work, but the old decision can no longer authorise its publication. Checking the new decision might require changing one sentence, recasting the page as a historical account or abandoning it. We have to read what changed to know which.

Record what the draft depends on

The proposed protocol has five operations: open a transaction for the relevant scope, query its context, propose a change, respond to that proposal and watch the dependencies. The record of what was read includes the source revisions, which items belonged to the scope and who had authority over the decision. Those last two can change even when the wording stays the same.

A records that its draft used availability decision r1 within the scope where that decision applies. B proposes r2 through the scope's designated writer; the design permits only that writer to make the accepted change. Once r2 is accepted, A's watch reports that its dependency has changed. Before publication, the proposal must be checked against r2. Cancellation, abort and expiry also have explicit outcomes. Silence cannot stand in for a successful response.

Four consistency choices describe different uses of this record:

Consistency class What the reader asks for
Snapshot A coherent account at the selected revision
Causal The declared dependency order, so a derived result does not precede the ground it used
Strong A fresh check of the visible source revisions, scope and authority before the next consequential step
Speculative Continued reasoning whose changed ground has not yet been reconciled

Note

These names describe consistency guarantees. Here “causal” means respecting the declared dependency order, not identifying scientific causes. A “strong” check can confirm that the visible context is current; it cannot prove the claims in that context true.

One writer per scope and a fixed ordering rule where scopes overlap would make it possible to replay the same changes and get the same result. The experiment must show whether those rules catch the stale dependency more precisely, or at less cost, than the simpler version-checking system.

Version order is not semantic truth

A revision records an accepted change and its place in the history. It does not prove that the newer wording is true, that its author had the relevant authority or that every dependent claim must change. Those questions still belong to the source and its decision process.

Agents on unrelated work should not wait for each other

While A revises the service page, agent C may be working on an unrelated essay. C should keep going without waiting for one global agent to approve everyone's next step. Where scopes overlap, the system needs a rule for rejecting conflicting changes or applying them in order. It must also record changes in membership and authority: moving a source into a different scope, or changing who can decide, can invalidate A's use of it even if its paragraph is unchanged.

Context consistency does not execute the effect

Checking r2 answers whether A's draft still rests on a current decision. The publisher separately decides whether it may go out. The system that performs publication keeps its credentials, checks permission and records what happened.

If a publication request was sent but its response was lost, rereading r2 cannot tell us whether the page went live. That unknown external effect needs a check of the provider's state and a way to recover without blindly repeating the action. Scope would identify what reasoning needs another look; the system that performed the action must establish what it actually did.

One changed premise, two agents

The first experiment can follow this case all the way through. A reads the availability decision, B changes it, and the check stops A's next attempted publication before anything goes out. A still has its draft to revise. Replaying the same sequence reaches the same result, while C's unrelated work continues.

The case, moment by moment:

Moment in the proposed experiment Agent A Agent B Unrelated agent C
Initial read Uses availability revision r1 Prepares a change to that decision Works within another scope
Source revision Its draft still contains the r1 claim Records the accepted revision r2 Continues
Revalidation Detects the changed premise and revises or retains speculative work Its change remains in the source history Does not acquire a dependency on r2 merely by running concurrently

Run that case against the simpler versioned resolver and compare what each detects, what it unnecessarily stops and how much coordination it costs. Explicit semantic dependencies earn their place only if they improve that comparison. The useful result is that A knows which part of its work to reconsider and C has no reason to stop.

entry.title: When context helps
entry.content:
When context helps

A context system learns very little from knowing that an agent opened a document. The document might have resolved an uncertainty, confirmed something already known or supplied a convincing distraction. The agent might quote it because it helped, or because it was the only thing returned. Useful memory begins with a harder question: what difference did this context make to the work?

That question drives the learning design for Scope. The aim is a system that gets better at choosing a small, useful account of a task, without accumulating every previous selection as evidence that the selection was good. Retrieval is part of a larger process. Its value appears in the understanding, decision or completed work that follows.

Four events, four possible stories

Imagine a support task. A product rule is required context. Two optional sources are also eligible: a recent troubleshooting note and a worked example for a particular device. The system returns the rule and the note; the agent reads both, quotes the note and resolves the issue.

The record establishes that the note was offered, consumed and mentioned. A separately observed resolution establishes that the task ended successfully. It does not yet establish that the note caused the success. The agent may already have known the answer. The note may have been redundant with the rule. The unseen device example may have led to the same result more quickly.

Those alternatives matter to learning. A model trained to predict what the incumbent retrieves can reproduce the incumbent's habits, including its mistakes. A model trained on mentions can reward sources that are easy to quote. A model trained on consumption can favour attractive opening material over the quiet qualification that prevents an error. Each target is learnable; none is automatically the target we wanted.

The record therefore needs the eligible alternatives and the information available when the choice was made, alongside the later use and outcome. An unselected item remains an unobserved alternative, not a failed source. The timing also matters: a feature known only after the task ended cannot explain a choice that must be made before it begins.

For this task, a compact learning record would retain these separate observations:

At selection time During the attempt At evaluation
Required product rule; eligible note and device example; chooser and its choice probability where defined Returned bundle; passages consumed; passages mentioned Resolution result; independently checked errors; elapsed time and resources

The chooser needs a record too. A deterministic rule selecting the note every time gives that choice probability one and the alternative zero. An experiment could deliberately give each alternative a nonzero chance of selection, after deciding which tasks and assignments are safe to try. These histories support different comparisons even if both end with a successful task.

The missing observation

Suppose the same deterministic rule always returns the troubleshooting note for this kind of task. A thousand successful cases can tell us something about that complete workflow. They cannot show what those cases would have looked like with the device example instead. There are no outcomes for that choice in those cases.

Off-policy evaluation studies precisely this partial-feedback problem: using decisions made by one policy to assess another. Li and colleagues' offline evaluation work uses randomised logging to make a principled comparison possible. Wang, Agarwal and Dudík examine the statistical limits and trade-offs of contextual-bandit evaluation. A retrieval bundle is more complicated than choosing one news article, so the assumptions and action definition cannot simply be borrowed unchanged.

The elementary obstacle survives that difference. In an inverse-propensity calculation, an observed outcome is weighted according to how likely its action was under the logging policy. If an alternative had zero probability of being selected, weighting cannot manufacture an observation of it. Better estimators can address some variance or modelling problems; they do not turn a never-tried alternative into an independently observed outcome.

A comparison small enough to understand

One candidate need not be a neural model. A simple baseline can score an eligible item by recency times the logarithm of one plus its previous retrieval count. That rule gives a never-retrieved item zero even when it is fresh: a concrete cold-start behaviour to compare, rather than a vague claim that popular material is helpful. The recency function and candidate-time counts must be fixed for the experiment.

Scope's initial design, A-MAC-lite, instead combines a content-kind prior, access recency, a declining novelty boost and a multiplier from accepted reports of use. That makes its preference inspectable, but does not turn the ranking into a probability of truth or usefulness. Four reports of use are not evidence that an item caused four successes. Neither access recency nor the score can restore an expired source to eligibility.

A moving-average candidate goes further by updating utility from a declared credit and outcome feature. It would make a preference based on reported use and an outcome-attribution rule compete on the same tasks. Mentions, controlled ablations and owner-observed outcomes supply different grounds for credit; none should quietly replace the others. The task outcome remains a vector of observations. Reducing it to one feature is a particular experiment's choice, not a declaration that every successful task is worth one. A scorer that learns the wrong reduction can become very good at choosing context for the wrong objective.

A first experiment could hold the required product rule fixed and compare the optional context on a fixed set of tasks whose owners permit the experiment. One arm uses a simple recency-and-frequency score; another uses the proposed richer scorer. Both receive the same source population, task conditions and context budget. The required rule is not sacrificed to create an impressive token saving.

In a controlled offline setting, the task can be rerun with different optional bundles. That directly measures the selected agent's behaviour in that setting. It is stronger evidence than rescoring yesterday's choices, but still depends on the task sample, executor, evaluation and fidelity of the replay. In a live setting, deliberate exploration needs its own safe assignment design; the fact that an alternative is eligible does not make every experiment with it harmless.

The outcome is more informative as several observations than as one triumphant score. Did the issue resolve? Did an independent check find an error? How much time and resource did it take? Was essential information lost? A faster answer that fails on the difficult device is a different trade-off from an equally correct answer that saves time everywhere. The comparison needs enough separation to see which one happened.

It also needs new situations. A scorer can learn one operator's language or recognise near-duplicate tasks without learning a useful retrieval rule. Future time windows and held-out operators test that dependence. If the simpler scorer performs equivalently under the relevant conditions, extra learning machinery has not earned its cost.

A memory that becomes more useful

More elaborate ranking, credit assignment or history models become interesting when a simpler method leaves a specific failure unexplained. Perhaps the value of a source depends on the preceding context, or a short sequence reveals that a recurring answer has stopped helping. That is a reason to test a richer representation, not an automatic promotion from a good replay to a self-changing memory.

Reckon’s completed selective-memory comparisons make the cost of choosing visible. A policy improved over learned utility in one workload while losing to no memory; in another, it matched a simpler policy’s wins after paying for thousands of extra replays. The work spent deciding what to remember belongs in the comparison too.

Those results give Scope questions to test on its own tasks. Scope would propose a retrieval change; an evaluation and its owner’s decision would precede any release of that change. Ordinary strict retrieval need not wait for an evaluation service to be online.

The resulting memory would preserve a productive distinction: a source can be frequently useful without being true in every setting, and rarely used while remaining indispensable for a particular decision. Eligibility determines what may enter the comparison. Evidence from the work determines what the comparison can teach. The gain is not a larger history of reading; it is a shorter, better-grounded route through the next task.

{"images":[],"notes":{"body_html":"

Three scores for an eligible source

A score can be easy to calculate while carrying a quite different idea of usefulness from its competitors. These worked examples expose that difference. The inputs are stipulated, not measured retrieval results. Eligibility is settled before any of these calculations: an expired or excluded source cannot re-enter the response by scoring well.

Recency and frequency

The simple baseline is recency times the logarithm of one plus the previous retrieval count. For a recency value of 0.5 and three prior retrievals:

b=0.5ln⁡(1+3)≈0.693. b=0.5\ln(1+3)\approx0.693.

An item with recency 1 and no retrievals scores zero under this formula. That is its cold-start behaviour, not proof that the item cannot help. The recency function and candidate-time counts are part of the experiment's fixed definition.

A-MAC-lite's components

Scope's proposed defaults give a transaction item prior 0.5 and a 30-day access half-life. Give an eligible item thirty days since access, two prior retrievals and four accepted reports that the item was used. Its recency is 0.5, novelty is 1−2/5=0.61-2/5=0.6, and support from those reports is 4/10=0.44/10=0.4. The raw score becomes:

s=0.5×0.5×(1+0.3×0.6)×(0.5+0.5×0.4)=0.2065. s=0.5\times0.5\times(1+0.3\times0.6)\times(0.5+0.5\times0.4)=0.2065.

Dividing by the configured maximum 1.3 gives approximately 0.159. That is a ranking value, not a probability that the source is true or helpful. Normalisation belongs to this active configuration; a different prior or weight changes its maximum. The reported-use multiplier is narrower than outcome utility: four reports of use do not establish four caused successes.

Note

The illustrative baseline value and this normalised score are not comparable magnitudes. They arise from different rules and scales. The useful comparison is the bundles they select under the same conditions and what happens in the ensuing work.

A moving-average utility

Scope's proposed comparison includes a moving-average candidate referenced from Reckon's research:

unew=(1−η)uold+η c o,η=0.1, u_{new}=(1-\eta)u_{old}+\eta\,c\,o, \qquad \eta=0.1,

with the result clamped to the unit interval. Here cc is the credit assigned under the experiment's rule and oo its specified outcome feature. With illustrative values uold=0.4u_{old}=0.4, c=0.5c=0.5 and o=1o=1, the next utility is 0.36+0.05=0.410.36+0.05=0.41. If that outcome feature is zero, it becomes 0.36.

Neither update establishes causation. It shows how a declared attribution rule changes future preference. Mentions, controlled ablations and owner-observed outcomes can produce different credit, which is why the comparison preserves them separately. The task outcome remains a vector of relevant observations; reducing it to oo is this experiment's choice, not a universal definition of a successful task.
